records.summary: 767 Bush St is in the RC-4 (Residential Commercial, High Density) zoning district where a restaurant is principally permitted on the ground floor as a Retail Sales and Service use. No prior permits or applications are on file at this address. The site sits in an extremely dense food and beverage corridor: 33 registered food or drink businesses and 26 active ABC on-sale licenses within 500 feet, signaling high undue-concentration risk if alcohol were added later. The immediate block has seen consistent approvals for restaurant uses over the past decade, including two new restaurants with alcohol approved in May 2022 at 550 and 560 Powell (115 m away), both in RC-4 zoning.

No site history: Zero permits, applications, or ABC licenses on file at 767 Bush St or parcel 0284/018

ABC license conditions are not exposed in the data for the 34 active licenses within 500 ft

comparables.why_comparable: New restaurant (Bellini) with ABC Type 47 full-bar license at 550 Powell St, 115 m away, same RC-4 zoning district, approved May 2022. Agency referral for ABC license.
comparables.key_takeaway: Planning approved a new restaurant with full liquor service on the same block in RC-4 zoning within 5 days, explicitly citing PC Section 209.3 (restaurant principally permitted at ground level). The record notes 'continuation of existing use,' meaning the space was already food/beverage, unlike this dry-cleaner conversion.

comparables.why_comparable: New restaurant (Piranesi) with ABC Type 41 beer-and-wine license at 560 Powell St, 115 m away, same RC-4 zoning district, approved May 2022. Agency referral for ABC license.
comparables.key_takeaway: Approved simultaneously with Bellini at 550 Powell (same filing and decision dates), demonstrating Planning's routine approval of restaurant uses with alcohol in RC-4 on this corridor. Both were agency referrals, not discretionary hearings, confirming restaurants are by-right.

comparables.why_comparable: Restaurant (Key Club) with ABC Type 41 beer-and-wine license transfer at 850 Bush St, 139 m away, same RC-4 zoning district, approved November 2021. Agency referral.
comparables.key_takeaway: Another RC-4 restaurant approval on Bush Street itself, directly comparable to the subject site. Approved in 12 days for an ABC referral. Record notes 'continuation of existing use,' so also a food-to-food succession.

comparables.why_comparable: Limited restaurant at 878 Bush St, 172 m away, same RC-4 zoning district, approved July 2021. DPH health permit referral.
comparables.key_takeaway: Approved in 19 days. Planning explicitly cited PC Section 209.3 and called it 'continuation of existing use,' showing routine health-permit zoning sign-offs for restaurant uses in RC-4. This was a change-of-ownership referral, not a change of use from a non-food space.

comparables.why_comparable: Limited restaurant (Acai R) at 891 Bush St, 171 m away, same RC-4 zoning district, approved November 2020. DPH health permit referral.
comparables.key_takeaway: Approved in 13 days. Another RC-4 approval on Bush Street citing PC Section 209.3. Address has had three restaurant approvals in the records (2019, 2020, 2021), showing established food-use pattern on the corridor.

comparables.why_comparable: New ABC Type 41 license for restaurant (Estela's) at 891 Bush St, 171 m away, same RC-4 zoning district, approved September 2019. Agency referral.
comparables.key_takeaway: Approved in 98 days (longer than typical ABC referrals), but still approved without conditions. Confirms RC-4 permits restaurant with beer and wine by right under PC Section 209.3. Same address later saw two more restaurant approvals, showing sustained food-use continuity.

comparables.why_comparable: Restaurant health permit at 650 Bush St, 169 m away, same RC-4 zoning district, approved May 2018. DPH referral.
comparables.key_takeaway: Approved in 7 days with no extracted conditions. Minimal description, but fast approval demonstrates straightforward DPH-to-Planning referrals for restaurant uses in RC-4 when the prior use was also food/beverage.

comparables.why_comparable: Restaurant (L'Ottavo) with ABC Type 41 at 692 Sutter St, 185 m away, different zoning (C-3-G Downtown General), approved September 2022. Agency referral.
comparables.key_takeaway: Approved in 2 days. While C-3-G is a different district, it confirms Planning's consistent practice of routine ABC-referral approval for restaurants. Record notes 'continuation of existing use,' so another succession within the same use category.

patterns.pattern: Restaurant use in RC-4 zoning on Bush/Powell corridor is universally approved when the prior use was already food/beverage. All seven RC-4 restaurant approvals within 200 m (550 Powell, 560 Powell, 650 Bush, 850 Bush, 878 Bush, 891 Bush ×3) were decided within 2–19 days for health/ABC referrals and described as 'continuation of existing use.'

Planning Code Section 209.3 expressly permits restaurant as a Retail Sales and Service use on the ground floor in RC-4 by right, without discretionary review. Every RC-4 restaurant approval in the candidate set cited this section and was processed as an agency referral (health or ABC), not a use decision or CUA.

No conditions or operating restrictions were imposed on any of the approved restaurant referrals in RC-4. All approvals came with zero extracted conditions, suggesting agency referrals for permitted uses receive pro-forma approval without mitigation measures.

Restaurants with alcohol (ABC Types 41 and 47) are approved as readily as restaurants without alcohol in RC-4. Four of the seven RC-4 comparables involved ABC licenses (two Type 41, one Type 47, one unspecified Type 41), all approved without additional conditions.

Change-of-use approvals from prior food/beverage to new restaurant are processed identically to change-of-ownership cases. The records describe even ownership changes as 'continuation of existing use' and approve them within 2–19 days through agency referrals, not discretionary review.

approval_signals: Restaurant use in RC-4 zoning per PC Section 209.3 (principally permitted)
Ground-floor location in a Retail Sales and Service corridor
High concentration of existing food/beverage uses nearby (33 within 500 ft) normalizes restaurant use
No alcohol proposed (avoids ABC undue-concentration review in this high-density tract)
Consistent approval pattern on Bush St and Powell St within 200 m
No laundromat or other protected prior use that would trigger PC Section 202.12
denial_signals: Prior use as a laundromat would trigger PC Section 202.12 CUA requirement (applicable to this site if the dry cleaner is classified as protected service)
Applying for bar use (ABC Type 42/48) instead of restaurant might require CUA hearing even if by-right
Any change from a protected service (laundromat, automotive) requires discretionary approval

risk.concept_summary: A restaurant with full commercial kitchen, five employees, and tenant improvements at 767 Bush St in San Francisco's RC-4 zoning district, converting from a prior dry cleaner use.

overall.next_step: Confirm with Planning whether the business is part of a chain (formula retail) and provide the floor area in square feet; these two inputs are required to determine whether a Conditional Use Authorization hearing is needed or the restaurant is permitted by right.

approvals.summary: The rules could not decide whether a use authorization is needed because the description does not state whether the business is part of a chain (formula retail) or the floor area of the restaurant.

findings.text: Restaurant use in RC-4 zoning is principally permitted on the ground floor as a Retail Sales and Service use under Planning Code Section 209.3, which has been in force since before 2022.

Two new restaurants with alcohol licenses were approved on the same block in May 2022 (550 Powell and 560 Powell, 115 m away) in RC-4 zoning, both as agency referrals decided within 5 days citing PC Section 209.3.
RC-4 requires Conditional Use Authorization for formula retail establishments, but the description does not state whether this business is part of a chain.
RC-4 requires Conditional Use Authorization for uses of 6,000 square feet or more, but the description does not give the floor area.
The space was last used as a dry cleaner (other use), not a laundromat, so the laundromat conversion rule (PC Section 202.12) requiring CUA does not apply.

approvals.summary: Health permit to operate is allowed: it is issued after plan check and inspection without a discretionary hearing, and the application will be referred to Planning for zoning review.

findings.text: Every food or drink business in San Francisco needs a health permit to operate, issued by the Department of Public Health after plan check and final inspection.
DPH health permit applications for restaurants and bars are sent to Planning for zoning review as an interagency referral.
Seven RC-4 restaurant health permits within 200 m were approved as agency referrals in 2–19 days between 2018 and 2022, all citing PC Section 209.3 as principally permitted.

approvals.summary: Building permit with change of use is further review: a change of use needs a building permit that must conform to the Planning Code, and the building permit application will be routed to Planning for zoning review.

findings.text: A change of use from another use to restaurant requires a building permit under San Francisco Building Code Section 106A.1, and the permit must conform to the Planning Code before it is issued per PC Section 175.
Building permit applications are sent to Planning for zoning review under Planning Code Section 175(a).

The proposed occupancy group is not established because the description does not state whether the space is for fewer than 50 people; the existing occupancy group is not in public records and can only be determined by plans or an inspection.

Tenant improvements including a commercial kitchen hood, finishes, equipment, and ADA upgrades need a building permit with stamped plans from an architect, plus separate electrical, plumbing, and mechanical permits pulled by licensed subcontractors.

filing_playbook.action: Contact San Francisco Planning Department zoning counter to confirm formula retail status and floor area requirements.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: State that you are opening a restaurant at 767 Bush St in RC-4 zoning and need to confirm two things before filing: (1) whether your business qualifies as formula retail under PC Section 178.1 (provide your business name, concept, and any other locations or affiliations), and (2) the floor area threshold for Conditional Use Authorization (PC Section 209.3 states 6,000+ sq ft requires CUA). Ask whether the dry cleaner prior use is a protected service under PC Section 202.12 that would require CUA for conversion. Request written confirmation by email that restaurant use is principally permitted on the ground floor if you are not formula retail and under 6,000 sq ft.

filing_playbook.action: Form LLC or corporation with California Secretary of State and obtain federal EIN.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation (ARTS-GS, $100) online at bizfile.sos.ca.gov. Within 90 days, file the Statement of Information ($20 LLC, $25 corporation). Apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) at irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/apply-for-an-employer-identification-number-ein-online the same day; it is issued immediately and free. The entity name and EIN are required for the business registration, bank account, lease, and all city permits.

filing_playbook.action: Register the business with San Francisco Treasurer & Tax Collector and file fictitious business name (DBA) with the County Clerk.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Register online at sftreasurer.org/business within 30 days of starting business; the fee is tiered by gross receipts ($55–$95 for most new restaurants, plus $4 state fee). You will receive a Business Account Number (BAN) required by every other city department. If your public-facing name differs from the legal entity name, file a fictitious business name statement with the County Clerk in person or by mail ($60–$120), then publish once a week for four weeks in an approved newspaper and file proof of publication within 45 days. Banks and other agencies will ask for the filed FBN statement.

filing_playbook.action: Hire an architect to prepare building permit plans for tenant improvements, kitchen, and change of use.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Engage a San Francisco restaurant architect to prepare stamped plans for the commercial kitchen hood, finishes, equipment layout, ADA upgrades, and any structural or MEP changes. Submit DPH health plan check and DBI building permit applications at the same time so both departments review in parallel. The building permit application must show the existing and proposed occupancy groups and occupant load; the architect will determine these from code and the layout. Make sure the DBI routing includes Planning (automatic under PC Section 175), Health, Fire, Public Works (for grease interceptor), and any other agencies. Budget 21–60 days for DPH plan review and 14–120 days for building permit review and inspections.

filing_playbook.action: Submit DPH health plan check application with menu, equipment list, and scaled drawings.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Apply online at sfdph.org/dph/EH/Food with your BAN, EIN, and a federal tax ID. Include two sets of scaled plans showing equipment placement, finishes, hand sinks, prep areas, storage, and the menu describing preparation methods. DPH will assign a plan reviewer; schedule a pre-final inspection at ~80% completion and a final inspection at least two weeks before your target opening. The flat fee for a new restaurant is $2,207 (8 hours) as of FY 2026–27, with additional review at $276/hour. Approval is required before DBI will issue the building permit final.

filing_playbook.action: Obtain California seller's permit, workers' compensation insurance, and EDD employer registration.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Register for a seller's permit at onlineservices.cdtfa.ca.gov (free, often same-day). CDTFA may request a security deposit depending on projected sales. Register as an employer with EDD at edd.ca.gov/Payroll_Taxes within 15 days of paying wages; your payroll provider needs the EDD account number before the first pay run. Purchase workers' compensation insurance from a licensed carrier or State Compensation Insurance Fund (required from the first employee, even part-time); several city permits ask for proof of coverage. Set up organics (green bin) collection with your hauler to comply with SB 1383 before opening.

filing_playbook.action: Certify a food safety manager and enroll employees in food handler card and RBS training (if alcohol is added later).
filing_playbook.what_to_say: At least one owner or employee must pass an ANSI-accredited food safety certification exam (ServSafe, Prometric, NRFSP, or 360training) within 60 days of opening; the certificate ($100–$250, valid 5 years) is required at the DPH pre-opening inspection. Every employee who handles food must obtain a California Food Handler Card ($7–$15, 2-hour online course, valid 3 years) within 30 days of hire. If you add alcohol service later, every server and manager must complete RBS training within 60 days of hire ($3 registration + $10–$25 course); ABC inspects for the certification list.

filing_playbook.action: Apply for health permit to operate after final building and fire inspections.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Submit the permit to operate application online at sfdph.org/dph/EH/Food at least one month before opening, with your BAN, Location ID (LIN), EIN, and proof that a certified food safety manager is on staff. The $470 application fee (FY 2026–27) includes the initial inspection; the annual license fee for restaurants is $0 for 2026–28. Schedule the final health inspection after DBI and SFFD sign off; failed inspections (missing hand sinks, unsealed surfaces, no hot water) push openings by 2–3 weeks, so walk the space against the DPH checklist a week before. The permit is issued only after the final inspection passes; you cannot serve the public before it is issued.

timeline_cost.notes: The day range (14–120 days) and government cost range ($470–$1,000) cover the health permit to operate and building permit with change of use, the two approvals in the entitlement path, measured from application to approval when they are granted. The health permit alone is 14–45 days and $470–$1,000; the building permit is 14–120 days and $800–$15,000 depending on construction valuation. These figures assume the zoning status becomes 'allowed' after the two missing inputs (formula retail status and floor area) are confirmed. If either input triggers a Conditional Use Authorization hearing, add 120–300 days and $3,100–$15,000 for the CUA, and the overall timeline becomes 134–420 days. The cost range does not include construction, architect fees, equipment, or non-government expenses such as workers' compensation insurance premiums. The day count is the time to approval, not to denial or withdrawal; no figures are given for those outcomes because the concept is not proposed for denial.
